11926-washington-in-domestic-life-from-o:
Richard Rush's Washington in Domestic Life, published in 1857, draws on original letters and manuscripts to present Washington at home. Rush, in confiding the brief paper to his publishers, offers to bear any deficiency in the cost of publishing after their charges are defrayed. That is a modest preface to a modest book.

The study concentrates on character as shown in household matters: correspondence, manners, and the management of Mount Vernon, rather than on campaigns or presidencies. For readers who knew Washington mainly as general and president, Rush's domestic portrait supplied a different scale. It shows how a public man's private habits and letters reveal the temper behind his public decisions.
13517-in-bohemia-with-du-maurier-the-fir:
Felix Moscheles remembers Bohemian days with George du Maurier in this first series of reminiscences, with sixty-three original drawings by du Maurier of the artist's life in the fifties. Moscheles wrote his introduction and posted last proofs shortly before du Maurier's death reached him in Venice, turning sunshine to darkness.

Du Maurier could draw and Moscheles paint, du Maurier sing and Moscheles mesmerise, and both talk beautifully, making them bright stars in Carry's firmament. A drawing shows a double-bedded room in Brussels at eleven, with Bobtail washing a smutty face and Rag putting on tight boots while smoking three pipes. Moscheles writes affectionate, art-filled memories of youth.
19273-the-dead-men-s-song-being-the-stor:
Champion Ingraham Hitchcock wrote this 1914 Louisville volume on Young Ewing Allison and his poem The Dead Men's Song. Only two hundred and fifty copies were made, with facsimiles of manuscripts and a photograph of Allison. Walt Mason's line opens the book: a poet of such a song deserves knell and praise.

Hitchcock recalls Allison's office habits, his desk-cleaning parties spring and fall, dust, torn papers, and humming of Bing-Binger the Baritone Singer. Letters were boxed to a warehouse, not copied, yet always found. Readers get a warm literary memoir of a Kentucky poet and his circle.
21594-fred-fenton-on-the-crew-or-the-you:
Fred Fenton takes an oar in Allen Chapman's Fred Fenton on the Crew, a volume of the Fred Fenton Athletic Series. Riverport School's young oarsmen train for the big race, shown in the front picture. We win, the caption cries, as Riverport takes the race.

Fred's friend, known far and wide as Bristles for his upright mop of hair, shares the fun. Chapman also wrote the Tom Fairfield and Darewell Chums series for boys. School honour, hard practice, and rivals on the river drive the plot. The tale ends, as the picture promises, with the crew's triumph on the water.
31025-a-new-species-of-pocket-gopher-gen:
Robert J. Russell's 1957 paper names a new pocket gopher, Pappogeomys alcorni, from the high Sierra del Tigre in southern Jalisco, Mexico. Collector J. R. Alcorn had taken gophers across Jalisco, Nayarit, and Colima in 1949 and 1950, and three specimens from that isolated volcanic range proved distinct from their kin.

The type specimen, an adult female taken four miles west of Mazamitla at 6,600 feet in October 1950, anchors the description. It adds notes on its medium size, short naked tail, and skull form. Known only from the higher ground of the Sierra del Tigre, the species shows how a cut-off mountain range can hold a mammal found nowhere else.
31141-four-new-pocket-gophers-of-the-gen:
Robert J. Russell's 1953 paper names four new pocket gophers of the genus Cratogeomys from central Jalisco, Mexico. Two species, gymnurus and zinseri, had been known only from southern and far eastern Jalisco, until collector J. R. Alcorn secured specimens of both in the central part of the state, where study showed two undescribed subspecies of each.

The first described, Cratogeomys gymnurus tellus, rests on an adult female taken three miles west of Tala at 4,300 feet in June 1949, a large, pale, long-tailed gopher. Field costs were met by the National Science Foundation and the Kansas University Endowment Association, and the paper remains the formal record for these central Jalisco forms.
31224-geographic-distribution-of-the-poc:
J. Knox Jones Jr.'s 1953 paper revises the geography of the pocket mouse Perognathus fasciatus, published as volume 5, number 29 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, with seven figures. Osgood's 1900 revision had known two races, and Cary added a pale Wyoming form in 1911, but no important work had followed for forty years.

Thirteen Nebraska specimens from the state's northwest corner matched no known subspecies, prompting Jones to examine material from the whole range. He reduces Perognathus callistus, long treated as a full species, to a subspecies of fasciatus, and names a new subspecies from eastern Wyoming and adjacent Montana, South Dakota, and Nebraska.
34117-beowulf-an-introduction-to-the-stu:
R. W. Chambers's 1921 Cambridge study Beowulf opens the old poem to readers who want more than the tale itself. Part one weighs the history in the poem: the Geats and their kings, Heorot and the Danish kings, and the stories of Offa and Finn.

Later chapters test the Grendel fight against northern parallels, from Grettir to Bothvar Bjarki, and weigh theories of the poem's date, build, and Christian strains. Part two prints source texts, so readers can judge the claims against the records themselves. Chambers dedicates the volume to William Witherle Lawrence, whose printed work and letters aided him.
34359-morituri-three-one-act-plays-teja-:
Hermann Sudermann wrote Morituri, three one-act plays translated from the German by Archibald Alexander. Scribner's Sons published the book at New York in 1910. The three plays are Teja, Fritzchen, and The Eternal Masculine. The catalog title keeps their names and drops the book's own.

Morituri is Latin for those who are about to die, the words of gladiators before the emperor. Sudermann was among the most played German dramatists of his day. His short plays turn on soldiers, honor, and the pull between duty and feeling. Teja is a Gothic king facing the end of his people. The set shows his art in small compass. Grace Frank and Edith Wharton translated other Sudermann plays for the same publisher, a sign of his standing in America then.
36111-prophets-of-dissent-essays-on-maet:
Otto Heller, professor of modern European literature at Washington University in Saint Louis, wrote these essays on four prophets of dissent. Maeterlinck, Strindberg, Nietzsche, and Tolstoy stand in his title. Heller had already published studies of Ibsen and of modern German literature.

Each of his four subjects rebelled against the settled world of the nineteenth century: the mystic playwright, the tormented Swede, the hammer philosopher, and the prophet count. Heller reads them as voices of one great unrest, in clear American prose. Readers get the rebels of European letters gathered under one roof.
42623-camping-on-the-st-lawrence-or-on-t:
Camping on the Saint Lawrence is a story for boys by Everett Tomlinson. Lee and Shepard copyrighted it in 1899. This Boston edition dates to 1905. Shute drew the illustrations. Its subtitle places the boys on the trail of the early discoverers.

A preface states the author's aim. He takes young readers to one of the noblest rivers. They share the stirring life of its waters. They also feel the power of its first explorers' story. The events, he says, come largely from real occurrences. Chapters cover preparations and the journey down. The boys sail the river and make camp. Ben tries the canoe. Sport in Goose Bay follows.
45464-the-mormon-doctrine-of-deity-the-r:
B H Roberts defends Mormon teaching on God in a volume issued at Salt Lake City in 1903. The book prints his discussion with Van der Donckt on the being and nature of God. A discourse by Roberts on Jesus Christ as the revelation of God is added, along with a set of church statements on the same theme.

Inside, Roberts argues from Joseph Smith's first vision, in which two distinct personages appeared to the young prophet. He holds that God the Father and Jesus Christ are separate persons, each in human form, and that the Godhead is a council of three. The preface frames this teaching as a sharp break with what Roberts calls a fallen, formless view of God.
46451-nasby-in-exile-or-six-months-of-tr:
Nasby in Exile, by David R Locke, the creator of Petroleum V Nasby, was published at Toledo and Boston in 1882. Locke sailed from New York on May 14, 1881, on the City of Richmond, with a varied assortment of passengers intent on seeing Europe. Six of them formed a party and toured together for six months through England, Ireland, Scotland, France, Germany, Switzerland, and Belgium. The book collects the letters he wrote home to the Toledo Blade, profusely illustrated.

Locke's preface is cheerfully honest: no one asked for the book, and it is a purely mercantile speculation. The Nasby letters had made him America's favorite humorist of the dialect school. Here the humorist travels as himself, and the subtitle admits the result: six months of travel, with many things not of travel.
48700-on-cambrian-and-cumbrian-hills-pil:
Henry S Salt wrote On Cambrian and Cumbrian Hills, walks to Snowdon and Scafell in Wales and the Lake District. C W Daniel issued a revised edition in London in July nineteen hundred twenty two. The book first came out in nineteen hundred eight. A photo of Great Gable faces the title page.

Salt says grand peaks need not send men abroad to climb. Shape, not mere height, makes a true mountain, he argues. Skye and Arran prove his point in Scots stone. Snowdon and Scafell have ridge, mist, tarn, and storm in full. Snow and ice crown them in the cold months. Why pay guides in the Alps, he asks, for the same thrills at home? Wild life and bare slopes get fond chapters of their own.
49073-venezuela-an-economic-report-prese:
Venezuela: An Economic Report was presented by students of Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service and published by the university in Washington in April nineteen twenty-one. It stands as Series Two, Bulletin Number One, and the first of a planned series of economic surveys of the world's commercial areas. The frontispiece shows Venezuelan and Georgetown students together at the foot of a statue of Bolívar.

The report was meant as an aid to the foreign trade of the United States. It is dedicated to Esteban Gíl Borges, Venezuela's minister of foreign relations. Georgetown marked the occasion by conferring on him an honorary doctorate of laws that same April. Letters, receptions at Caracas, and a tour of northern Venezuela frame the survey work.
50738-geneva-painted-by-j-hardwicke-lewi:
Geneva belongs to a set of handsome Swiss travel books in which color paintings by the Lewis family carry the show. Twenty full-page pictures in color go with the text, in the manner of the companion volumes on Montreux and the Upper Engadine. The book presents the city on its lake for armchair travelers.

The chapters walk Geneva through its whole past: the old town, the cathedral, and the age of Theodore de Beze, Calvin's friend and heir. One chapter tells of the Escalade, the night attack by Savoy that Geneva still celebrates. Later ones reach revolutions and the city's fame in literature and science. It is a portrait of a small city with an outsized place in European history.
58174-the-battle-of-wavre-and-grouchy-s-:
The Battle of Wavre and Grouchy's Retreat is a study of a little-known part of the Waterloo campaign, by Hyde Kelly, an officer of the Royal Engineers. It was printed in London in 1905 with maps and plans. Kelly says the great battle itself has dazzled readers away from its tail end, the fight at Wavre and the French retreat after it.

Kelly follows Marshal Grouchy's moves against the Prussian force under Thielemann. He asks why Grouchy failed to join Napoleon at Waterloo, and how he then drew his army off in good order. Kelly argues that a campaign full of mistakes teaches as much as a clean one. The book suits readers who know the main battle and want the missing corner filled in.
59543-how-to-use-a-galvanic-battery-in-m:
Herbert Tibbits wrote How to Use a Galvanic Battery in Medicine and Surgery, a discourse delivered before the Hunterian Society. J and A Churchill published the third edition at London in 1886. Tibbits had been medical superintendent of the National Hospital for the Paralysed and Epileptic at Queen Square. He founded the West End Hospital for Diseases of the Nervous System. Three lectures on electro-therapeutics, given at the National Hospital, are worked into this edition.

The note to the third edition tells the book's purpose. Those who heard the discourse asked for it in print. Busy practitioners, they thought, would be glad to have the matter at hand in small compass. In so short a space, Tibbits owns, he could only recall the diseases where electricity has proved useful. He could not treat the whole subject.
62228-extracts-from-sikes-on-parochial-c:
An unnamed compiler made these extracts from Sikes on Parochial Communion, a scarce book on church order, and printed them at Oxford and London in 1864. The extracts treat bishops and the sin of schism, the splitting of the Church. The pages are dedicated, by leave, to the Lord Bishop of Oxford.

The preface says the source book was long out of print and too good to lose. The extracts argue that the priesthood holds a sacred character and a divine charge. If that were grasped, the compiler holds, many divisions that trouble the Church would end. The pamphlet also warns against the itch for change and for new ministers.
69466-a-few-days-in-athens-being-the-tra:
Frances Wright wrote A Few Days in Athens, shown here at Boston in 1850 as the English text of a Greek work said to be found at Herculaneum. Wright gives the book to Jeremy Bentham. She praises his clear thought, his useful work, and his kind acts. She thanks him for his friendship too.

Wright owns that a Greek scholar in Italy helped her with the text. She will not name him in full. She says harsh church rule in Italy forced scholars to hide their learning. A quote at the head links bliss and virtue in the way of Epicurus. The tale that follows spends a few days in old Athens and weighs how to live well.
doe-osti-3003144-self-consistent-relativ:
Sidharth Kannan, Evan Aubrey Semenak, David Tyler Markham, and colleagues at Los Alamos present a math-heavy study in report LA-UR-25-31121, issued in 2025. The topic is relativistic electron scattering in hot plasma, modeled with the Sherlock scattering approach. Scattering rates feed X-ray diagnostic simulations, which read plasma conditions from the X-rays a shot emits.

The team built a numerical scheme for the diffusion coefficients of the Beliaev-Budker operator, the relativistic collision operator. Benchmarks against the NIMROD code and Mathematica matched on the scalar potentials used. Against the older Papp approximation used in a Los Alamos code, the new model differs strongly at high temperature because it stays self-consistent with relativity. It runs slower, the authors note, but within a usable range for many applications.
doe-osti-3013860-providing-thermal-stabi:
David Grant, Chris DePrater, Natalie Bates, and co-authors from Oak Ridge, Lawrence Livermore, and Sandia wrote this case study, SAND2025-15409R, on keeping an exascale supercomputer cool. Frontier, Oak Ridge's exascale machine, swings its power draw violently during normal work. Its direct-liquid cooling loops respond over minutes, but component temperatures react in seconds, a mismatch that can force shutdowns or throttle performance.

The paper explains how Frontier's cooling plant handles the swings: watching computer power meters gives an earlier warning than temperature sensors, letting controls stage cooling towers ahead of the heat. Cooling demand runs about 284 ton-hours per megawatt-hour consumed. The authors translate watts into temperature targets with an adjustable gain so other centers can adapt the scheme, noting each design removes between 65 and 98 percent of heat by liquid.
doe-osti-3021212-blueprint-coordinated-v:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5T00-98193, by Katherine Amoresano, Myungsoo Jun, Jordan Smart, and Ryan Cryar, is a how-to blueprint for industry information-sharing groups that want to coordinate software vulnerability disclosure. When a researcher finds a flaw, coordinated disclosure routes the report to the affected vendors, who fix it before details go public. Sector groups known as ISACs increasingly field such reports but often lack a process.

The blueprint walks through intake, triage, and vendor notification, using the VINCE platform's reporting workflow as a working example. Reports are prioritized when they affect multiple vendors or touch safety, critical infrastructure, or national security. The authors adapt practices from mature disclosure programs to groups that are newer to receiving vulnerability reports. The goal is a repeatable process that vendors trust and researchers will actually use.
doe-osti-3023374-blueprint-coordinated-v:
Erich Feth, Katherine Amoresano, Myungsoo Jun, Jordan Smart, and Ryan Cryar of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this blueprint, report NLR/TP-5T00-97877, dated March 2026. It shows companies how to build a coordinated vulnerability disclosure program, the channel through which outside finders report security flaws so they get fixed instead of exposed. The worked examples target the electric vehicle charging industry.

A step-by-step guide walks charging equipment and vehicle makers through the process. Step one is intake: a finder submits a completed reporting form, and the company acknowledges receipt within three to five days. Later steps cover remediation and prioritization. The guide points readers to the top ten common weakness types for charging gear and includes a sample reporting form.
doe-osti-3347392-understanding-and-predi:
David R. Hatch of the University of Texas at Austin Institute for Fusion Studies reports final results on the pedestal of the NSTX spherical tokamak. The pedestal is the steep rim zone of hot plasma that sets much of a tokamak performance. The project hunted the instabilities that leak heat across that rim, then built a predictive model for the temperature profile there, checked against real NSTX shots.

Two very different discharges were matched with one recipe: electron-temperature-gradient turbulence, ion-scale kinetic ballooning transport, and standard neoclassical flow. One shot was a wide, quiet, lithium-coated pedestal; the other was narrow and bursty. A new finding is that magnetic flutter reshapes the electron turbulence near the pedestal top, right where measured pressure sits furthest below the ballooning limit. Machine learning tools also sorted turbulence regimes from simulation data.
doe-osti-3399495-collaborative-research-:
A four-university team closes award DE-SC0022012 with a final technical report on enabling multi-scale studies of magnetic reconnection with interpretable data-driven models. The period ran from September 1, 2021 to August 31, 2025. Frederico Fiuza of Stanford was lead principal investigator. Nuno Loureiro at MIT, E. Paulo Alves at UCLA, and William Dorland at the University of Maryland joined him. Reconnection is the sudden rearrangement of magnetic fields behind solar flares and tokamak disruptions.

The project goal was better reduced models: fluid descriptions that keep kinetic accuracy. The team built machine learning tools on sparse and symbolic regression. The tools pull readable equations, partial differential equations a physicist can inspect, out of first-principles particle simulation data. Earlier proof-of-principle work had recovered the known hierarchy of plasma equations from such data. Here the target was kinetic closures for reconnection, plus models of how reconnection injects and accelerates particles.
doe-osti-3484786-toward-next-generation-:
Argonne report ANL-26/32, dated July and August 2026, argues for next-generation support systems for scientific computing. Lois Curfman McInnes, Dorian Arnold, and Prasanna Balaprakash are among the many authors. Team science now spans fields, codes, and AI tools at once.

Cited sources trace decades of cyberinfrastructure planning reports. Cover images show fuel cooling clusters and a stellar explosion debris field. The report ties community, software, and AI into one ecosystem view. Labs planning future computing support get a shared agenda drawn from hard lessons learned in past national programs alike.
doe-osti-3682476-nuclear-data-covariance:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4734, dated August 2026, documents nuclear data covariance libraries built for the SCALE code suite. Eight authors are printed, led by Jesse M. Brown, Friederike Bostelmann, and Dorothea Wiarda. Covariance data say how unsure each nuclear data value is, and how those doubts link together. SCALE's sensitivity and uncertainty tools need such data to judge how much trust a reactor calculation deserves. The libraries serve SCALE 7.0.

Sources mix high-grade evaluations from ENDF/B-VIII.1 with rough uncertainty sets from a joint project. Brookhaven, Los Alamos, and Oak Ridge labs all took part in that joint work. Sections explain the low-fidelity data set, fission spectra data, and the step that folds values into energy groups. Two appendixes list each isotope entry and its source file in long tables. Provenance is traced for both ENDF editions, so users can see where each figure came from.
govdocs-archive_org-noob-flushyourmeds_N:
Scott A. Barry's NOOB #flushyourmeds is an e-book that mixes two subjects few books combine: beginner occult instruction and practical notes on digital privacy. Its title addresses the reader as a noob, a newcomer to both crafts at once.

Alongside occult material and numerology, Barry writes about MAC spoofing and routing traffic through Tor, the tools of staying anonymous online. The text is fragmentary and eclectic, jumping between its worlds without apology. The result is a strange hybrid from the internet's occult underground, where magic and operational security are treated as one art.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AllenMarkFOIASe:
When the House Select Committee on Assassinations took up the murders of John F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr. in the late 1970s, its members and staff needed a common base of background information. This briefing book was prepared for the committee to supply it.

The volume gathers the background the reinvestigation worked from, and it survives here as researcher Mark Allen's FOIA selection, drawn from disclosures dated April 12, 1984. Briefing books show what investigators were told before they began asking questions, which makes them evidence in their own right. The file is a public record of the second official inquiry.
in-bohemia-with-du-maurier-the-first-of-:
Felix Moscheles wrote this memoir of his student days with artist George du Maurier in the fifties. The London book holds sixty-three drawings by du Maurier that show that early life. Moscheles finished the proofs just before news of his friend's death reached him in Venice.

He chose to let the joyous pages stand as du Maurier had approved them. Music binds the friends in the tale, from Leipzig circles to a concert tour in Belgium. Pianist Louis Brassin links them to the master Moscheles. The book preserves a bohemian youth and a deep friendship in art.
nasa-tm-19680005116-parametric-analysis-:
James J. Ward and Robert Ruch, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, analyzed a nuclear power generator in January 1968. The machine turns heat from a radioisotope fuel block into electricity in two cascaded stages. A hot silicon-germanium stage sits inside, wrapped by a cooler lead telluride stage.

Heat leaves through the outer shell, and fins are usually needed to help it escape. Ward and Ruch vary the design parameters to see how performance changes. Such generators power spacecraft far from the Sun, where solar cells fail. The analysis maps the choices a designer must trade against each other.
nasa-tm-19710003531-experimental-determi:
Frank Bugg of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 20, 1970. It measures, by experiment, how fast liquid sloshes in a tilted round tank. The tank is a right circular cylinder set at an incline, like a propellant tank in a climbing rocket.

Bugg tilted the tank at four angles to the vertical and varied the liquid depth as well. Two slosh modes were tracked, told apart by which way the still line across the surface ran. Raising the tilt lowered the slosh frequency of both modes, he reports. The mode tied to the surface's minor axis slowed much more than the other.
nasa-tm-19720022221-s-cubed-a-spacecraft:
S-Cubed A, a Spacecraft and Experiment Description, is a NASA document on the Explorer 45 satellite, called S3-A before launch. The small scientific satellite launched on November 15, 1971, from the San Marco range in Kenya aboard a four-stage Scout rocket. It entered an elliptical equatorial orbit carrying charged particle and field experiments.

The S3 program gave experimenters a small, flexible spacecraft able to fly a well-integrated detector set on the economical Scout. Its data handling system was unusual for its time because it could be reprogrammed from the ground. This description sets out the first mission's scientific objectives, aimed at magnetospheric phenomena in the heart of the magnetosphere. It also defines the orbital parameters, summarizes detector characteristics, and explains the data system's capabilities.
podcast-dannyjones-y3XbBfTqcSc:
Wildlife host Forrest Galante joins Danny Jones to talk about DNA scientists who plan to build a real Jurassic Park by 2027. Galante is a biologist known for hunts for lost species. The plan at issue is de-extinction, the bid to bring back the dead.

Galante walks through the labs that aim to revive lost beasts from old DNA. He weighs which beasts could walk again first and what parks might hold them. Jones asks where the plan could go wrong. Listeners get a wild but real tale from the edge of gene work. The library files the talk as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson-DG-dcjlzCsc:
Tucker Carlson declares that the ruling class is losing control. His short title carries the whole thesis of the hour. He points to cracks in media, courts, and party power.

Carlson argues that elite panic shows in bans, suits, and harsh words. Each move, he says, admits that old tools fail. He urges viewers to read fear as a sign of change. The episode is a rallying brief for the hopeful and the rebellious. It gives no guest and no hedge: one host reads the moment as a turning of the tide.
the-dead-men-s-song-being-the-story-of-a: Champion Ingraham Hitchcock wrote The Dead Men's Song as the story of a poem and a sketch of its author, Young Ewing Allison, his friend. The Louisville edition of 1914 was limited to two hundred and fifty copies. Its title promises a browse through other gems of Allison's and recollections of days, with facsimiles of manuscripts folded in. A quote from Walt Mason holds that the man who wrote the poem should not go unknelled, unhonored, and unsung. Only the title pages and front matter are present here.
washington-in-domestic-life-from-origina:
Richard Rush wrote Washington in Domestic Life from original letters and manuscripts in 1857. A letter to his publishers, J. B. Lippincott and Company of Philadelphia, fronts the piece. He tells them plainly that he will answer for any shortfall in the cost of publishing, once their charges for doing the work fitly are paid. If the small piece should by some remote chance yield a profit, he directs that it go, however small, to the Washington Monument Fund.

He calls the work a literary trifle, hardly worth a dedication. Yet he dedicates it to Charles J. Ingersoll all the same. The idea took shape at a dinner at Ingersoll's table, where the new Vice-President, Mr. Breckenridge, sat among the guests. Rush, who had known the world of the early republic, draws on private papers to show Washington at home.
